title: Toilet and sanitation when water is off
def: When water is off, a toilet can be flushed by pouring a bucket of water into the bowl, or a lined bucket can be used as an emergency toilet to keep waste contained.
look: a stored bucket of non-drinking water
use: Pour about a gallon of water quickly into the bowl to flush, or line a bucket with two bags, add cat litter or sawdust after use, seal, and store away from living space; wash hands every time.
not: Do not flush if the sewer is backing up or the area is flooded, and do not use drinking water for flushing if supplies are short.

title: Storing drinking water at home
def: A common rule is to store at least one gallon of water per person per day for several days, in clean, food-grade containers kept cool and dark.
look: sealed store-bought water or clean food-grade jugs
a date written on each container
extra for pets and hot weather
use: Store at least a three-day supply, replace self-filled water about every six months, and keep containers away from chemicals and sunlight.
not: Do not reuse milk jugs or containers that held chemicals.

title: Is the refrigerator food still safe after an outage?
def: A closed refrigerator keeps food safe about 4 hours and a full closed freezer about 48 hours; after that, perishable food above 40°F for over 2 hours should be thrown out.
look: how long the power was out
ice crystals still in frozen food
use: Keep doors closed, check temperatures when power returns, refreeze food that still has ice crystals or is at 40°F or below, and discard warm perishables.
not: Do not taste food to decide if it is safe; when in doubt, throw it out.

title: Keeping phones charged in an outage
def: In an outage, save phone battery with low-power mode and limited use, and recharge from power banks, a car, or solar chargers.
use: Turn on low-power mode, text instead of calling, close apps, and charge from a power bank or a running car in an open area.
not: Do not run a car in a closed garage to charge a phone.

title: Never plug a generator into a wall outlet
def: Backfeeding, plugging a generator into a wall outlet or the panel without a transfer switch, can send power into the lines and kill utility workers or neighbors.
look: a cord with plugs on both ends
use: Plug appliances directly into the generator with outdoor-rated cords, or have an electrician install a transfer switch.
not: Do not plug a generator into a household outlet or connect it to the panel yourself.

title: Storing gasoline and fuel safely
def: Gasoline and other fuels should be stored in approved containers, outside living spaces, away from heat and flame, and in small amounts.
look: a detached shed or well-ventilated area
use: Store fuel in approved cans away from the house, keep propane tanks outdoors upright, and let engines cool before refueling.
not: Do not store fuel in the house or basement, or refuel a hot generator.

title: Staying cool in a heat wave without air conditioning
def: During extreme heat, fans alone may not prevent heat illness; cooling centers, cool showers, shade, and water lower the risk.
look: older adults, babies, or ill people at home
use: Go to an air-conditioned place or cooling center during the hottest hours, drink water, take cool showers, close blinds by day, and check on others.
not: Do not rely on a fan in very high heat, and never leave anyone in a parked car.

title: Using a wood stove or fireplace safely
def: Wood stoves and fireplaces need a clean, inspected chimney, dry wood, clearance from things that burn, and working smoke and CO alarms.
look: a screen and 3 feet of clear space
use: Burn only dry wood, keep a screen in place, store ashes in a covered metal can outdoors, and test smoke and CO alarms.
not: Do not burn trash or treated wood, use gasoline to start a fire, or leave a fire unattended.

title: Basement flooding or a failed sump pump
def: A flooded basement can hide electrical shock danger; power to the area should be off before anyone steps into the water.
look: water near outlets, the panel, or appliances
use: Stay out of standing water until power to the basement is shut off by the main breaker from a dry spot or by the utility; then pump out, dry, and clean.
not: Do not walk into flooded basements with live power, or run gas pumps or generators indoors.

title: Well water after a flood
def: A private well that was flooded may be contaminated and should not be used for drinking until it is disinfected and tested.
look: floodwater over or near the wellhead
use: Use bottled or boiled water, contact the local health department for testing and disinfection guidance, and test again before drinking.
not: Do not drink, cook with, or brush teeth with well water after flooding until it tests safe.

title: Important documents and cash for emergencies
def: Copies of IDs, insurance, medical records, and some small bills make it easier to evacuate, get help, and recover after a disaster.
look: small bills when card systems are down
use: Keep copies of IDs, insurance, prescriptions, deeds, and contacts in a waterproof pouch with your kit, plus some cash.
not: Do not keep the only copies at home where a fire or flood could destroy them.

title: Testing smoke and CO alarms
def: Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms should be tested monthly, batteries changed as the maker says, and units replaced about every 10 years.
look: a chirp that means a low battery
the date printed on the alarm
alarms on every level and outside sleeping areas
use: Press the test button monthly, replace batteries or the unit when it chirps, and replace alarms older than 10 years.
not: Do not remove batteries to silence a chirp and forget to replace them.

title: Burst pipe: shutting off the water
def: When a pipe bursts, shutting the main water valve quickly limits damage; it is often where the water line enters the house.
look: the main valve near the meter or entry point
use: Turn off the main water valve, shut off power to wet areas if it is safe to reach the breaker, open a faucet to drain, and call a plumber.
not: Do not touch electrical items while standing in water.

title: Stuck in a car in snow
def: If stranded in a vehicle in a snowstorm, it is usually safest to stay with the car, keep the exhaust pipe clear, and run the engine only briefly for heat.
use: Stay in the car, tie a bright cloth to the antenna, clear the exhaust pipe, run the engine about 10 minutes each hour with a window cracked, and move arms and legs to stay warm.
not: Do not walk away into a storm or run the engine with a blocked exhaust.
call: Call 911 if you are stranded and can get a signal.

title: Car won't start in the cold
def: Cold weather weakens car batteries; a jump start, done in the right order, often gets the car going.
look: jumper cables or a jump pack
use: Connect red to the dead battery's positive, red to the good positive, black to the good negative, and black to bare metal on the dead car away from the battery; start the good car, then the dead one.
not: Do not jump a cracked or leaking battery, or let the clamps touch each other.
